title: Suffix Alarm
statement: A log scanner watches a stream of lowercase letters that arrive one at a time. It has a list of forbidden words. After each arriving letter, report whether some forbidden word is a suffix of everything received so far, meaning the word's letters match the most recent letters of the stream, in order. Given the forbidden words and the whole stream as a string, return an array with one boolean per letter.
constraints: Each word is 1 to 20 lowercase letters, and words may repeat
0 <= stream.length <= 10000, and the stream contains only lowercase letters

examples.explanation: After "stap" the suffix "tap" is forbidden; after "stape" the suffix "pe" is; "stapep" ends in nothing forbidden; "stapepy" ends in "y". The first three letters have no match.
After "a" no word ends the stream; after "ab" both "ab" and "b" are suffixes, so one alarm is enough.

hints.content: After a letter arrives, only the end of the stream matters: a forbidden word of length L is checked against the last L letters.
Checking every word at every position works, but costs (number of words) times (word length) for each letter.
A word is a suffix of the stream exactly when the word read backwards equals the stream's end read backwards. So compare starting from the newest letter and move toward older letters.

Put the reversed words in a trie. For each arriving letter, walk down the trie following the stream from the newest letter backwards, stopping at the first mismatch or after the longest word's length.
Mark the trie node where a reversed word ends. If the walk lands on a marked node, report true for this letter. Each letter costs at most the length of the longest word.

testCases.explanation: Two words matching at the same moment.
An empty stream has no letters to report on.
A one-letter word matches every letter.
Overlapping matches: the word ends at positions 2 and 4.
A word and its own suffix are both forbidden.
The longest allowed word (20 letters) against a stream of the same length.

Words cut from repetitive runs and random noise over a three-letter alphabet: 40 words of 6 to 20 letters (5 of them 20 letters long) against a 6000-letter stream; about 50% of the letters raise the alarm, so ignoring long words or truncating the look-back changes the answer.

A big mixed workload over the full alphabet, with 250 random decoy words among the cut ones: 1000 words of 6 to 20 letters (86 of them 20 letters long) against a 9000-letter stream; about 49% of the letters raise the alarm, so ignoring long words or truncating the look-back changes the answer.

solutions.title: Compare every word against every position
solutions.intuition: For each new letter, test each forbidden word against the end of the stream so far.
solutions.approach: For each end position, loop over all words and check that the stream contains the word starting at end + 1 - word.length. Stop at the first match.
solutions.pseudocode: for end in stream: hit = any(word == stream[end+1-len(word) .. end] for word in words)
solutions.timeComplexity: O(stream * words * L) for words of length up to L
commonMistakes: Slicing the whole prefix for every letter, which makes the loop quadratic in the stream length.
Letting the start index go negative and matching a wrapped string.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This is the direct reading: for every letter, ask every word whether it ends here. It performs up to (number of words) comparisons per letter, each costing up to the word length, which is too slow for long streams.

steps.title: Letter 'p' in "stap"
steps.content: The word "tap" starts at index 1 and matches, so the alarm fires.

steps.title: Letter 'p' in "stapep"
steps.content: Neither "tap", "pe" nor "y" ends at index 5, so there is no alarm.

solutions.title: Reversed trie walked backwards from the newest letter
solutions.intuition: Suffix matching is prefix matching on the reversed strings, and a trie answers prefix questions one character at a time.
solutions.approach: Insert every word reversed into a trie, marking where each word ends. For each arriving letter, walk from the newest letter toward older ones, following trie edges, and stop at a missing edge, at a marked node (alarm), or after the longest word's length letters.
solutions.pseudocode:
trie = {} ; for w in words: insert reversed(w), mark end
for end in stream: node = root
  for i = end down to max(0, end - longest + 1): node = node.child[stream[i]]; if none: break; if node.marked: alarm; break
solutions.timeComplexity: O(total word letters) to build; O(L) per arriving letter, where L is the longest word (at most 20), so O(stream * L) overall
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(total word letters * 26) for the typed-array trie
commonMistakes: Inserting the words forward and then trying to match the stream forward, which tests prefixes instead of suffixes.
Not stopping at the longest word's length, so each letter scans back to the start of the stream.
Forgetting to stop at the first marked node when a shorter word already matches.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A word is a suffix of the stream exactly when its reverse is a prefix of the stream read backwards. So I build a trie of reversed words, and for each arriving letter walk it from the newest letter backwards. The walk can never be longer than the longest word, so each letter costs O(L) and the trie costs O(total letters) memory. Aho-Corasick would bring the per-letter cost to amortized O(1) by adding failure links, at the price of a more complex build; with words of at most 20 letters the reversed trie is the practical answer.

steps.title: Build the reversed trie
steps.content: For ["tap", "pe", "y"] the paths are p-a-t, e-p and y, each ending at a marked node.

steps.title: Letter 'p' in "stap"
steps.content: Walking back from 'p' goes p, a, t, landing on the end of "tap": alarm.

steps.title: The rest of "stapepy"
steps.content: 'e' then 'p' ends the path of "pe": alarm; the second 'p' finds no edge after 'e'; 'y' lands on a marked node. Output: false, false, false, true, true, false, true.
